title: Data centers' 'flexible' power usage could save the grid billions. Can they scale?
key_facts: Tech companies and utilities are exploring 'demand response': data centers temporarily cut or shift electricity use at times of peak demand or grid stress.
EPRI: US data center use could rise from about 177 to 192 TWh in 2024 to 383 to 793 TWh by 2030; surveyed data centers reported 10% to 30% peak reduction potential.
A Duke University Nicholas Institute study estimated flexibility could save $40 billion to $150 billion in capital investment over a decade.
So far mostly pilots or one-off deals; OpenAI agreed to cut grid draw by up to 1 GW from a planned 3.2 GW Georgia facility during stress periods.
Federal regulators in June ordered grid operators to consider new connection rules, including faster routes for flexible facilities.
Last month Google, NVIDIA and Emerald AI launched the AI Energy Management Alliance.
BMI analyst: scaling curtailment deals across hundreds of facilities needs significant capital spending and coordinated policy.
quote_evidence: The strategy, called “demand response”, involves data centers temporarily reducing or shifting electricity use during periods of peak demand or grid stress
A study by Duke University’s Nicholas Institute estimated that greater flexibility from data centers could save between $40 billion and $150 billion in capital investments over the next decade.
So far, the “demand response” strategy for data centers has mostly been deployed through pilot projects or one-off agreements.
why_it_matters_hint: Flexibility could ease grid strain and speed connections, but is unproven at scale.
